subject: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody
messages:
From: Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
To: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@carewell.com
Date: Sun, 3 Aug 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Hi David,

Thanks for taking this. We're reviewing your standard DPA and there are two operational asks from our security team before procurement can greenlight the SOW:

1) Ephemeral sessions / interactive chat: we need a short clause that guarantees interactions submitted by our users will be treated as ephemeral by default (retained only for the session and not used for model improvement) and a description of the redaction controls you offer for PII before any non-ephemeral logs are created.

2) Subprocessor chain-of-custody: our auditors want an auditable chain showing which subprocessors touch session data and a short process for emergency export/forensic access if we certify an incident.

Can you provide proposed DPA language and the operational evidence you can deliver (sample audit log snippet, subprocessor inventory, and a timeline for any additional gating work)? We're trying to avoid a long negotiation — procurement would like something we can sign within two weeks.

Attachments: none on my side.

Laura Chen
Director, Security & Compliance
CareWell Health
laura.chen@carewell.com

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
To: Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 3 Aug 2025 10:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Laura — thanks for laying this out clearly. Looping in Marissa (ops) and Kimberly (legal/compliance) to provide the operational artifacts and a tight clause we can propose.

Preliminary answers:
- Ephemeral sessions: we can commit to "session-scoped retention" by default for interactive sessions (session-level KV is ephemeral, TTL-based GC). We already have a no-model-improvement flag at the request level we can surface in the API and log.
- Redaction: we support token-level redaction and client-side SDK hooks; we'll attach a brief draft that shows the redaction responsibilities (we redact by default for recognized PII categories, customers can opt-in to additional redaction patterns).
- Subprocessor chain-of-custody: we maintain a subprocessor registry and sign an operational attestation that lists who had access for a given date window. We can provide a one-off forensic export under a documented request workflow with an audit trail.

I'm attaching a short draft clause for your review (ephemeral-redaction-draft.docx). Marissa / Kimberly — can you add a minimal evidentiary pack (sample audit log, subprocessor inventory) and a suggested legal paragraph that binds us to the chain-of-custody workflow? Procurement asked for a two-week turn.

—David
David Kim
Senior Privacy Manager, Redwood Inference

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
Date: Mon, 4 Aug 2025 08:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Thanks David — attaching the operational artifacts we can share today (subprocessor-inventory-202508.pdf). A few operational notes for the clause:

- Audit logs: we can provide a redacted sample log showing timestamps, request-id, model variant, redaction-applied flag, and subprocessor-hop metadata. Logs are retained for 90 days by default, can be extended under contract if you need longer retention for audits.

- Ephemeral session handling: by default interactive sessions are stored in ephemeral KV with a TTL of 24 hours. We can extend to configurable TTLs per customer up to 30 days under an SOW.

- Redaction workflow: our pipeline includes automated PII classifiers (SSNs, credit card numbers, PHI patterns) plus a manual override queue for customers who request additional redaction patterns. Redactions are applied before anything is copied to longer-term telemetry.

- Chain-of-custody: each handoff to a subprocessor is recorded with a signed metadata token (internal id), retention window, and justification. For incident forensic export requests we require: POA, scope, and a secure transfer method (SFTP or customer-managed onshore KMS).

I'll mark up the clause doc with these operational constraints.

Marissa
Principal Product Ops, Redwood Inference

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
Date: Mon, 4 Aug 2025 11:20:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Laura — adding the legal paragraph we think balances operational needs with contract scope. Below is suggested DPA language we can include as an Annex: 

"Annex X — Ephemeral Sessions and Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody"
- Ephemeral Sessions: Redwood Inference shall treat interactive session data submitted via CareWell's API as session-scoped by default and shall not use such session-scoped data for model improvement or training unless CareWell provides an explicit opt-in instruction in writing. Session-scoped data retention defaults to 24 hours; retention may be extended by mutual agreement and fee schedule in an SOW.
- Redaction Controls: Redwood will provide automated redaction for commonly recognized PII categories and will support customer-provided redaction patterns. Redwood will document when redaction was applied in the per-request audit log.
- Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody and Forensic Access: Redwood will maintain a subprocessor registry and will, upon written request and appropriate authorization, provide an auditable export showing subprocessor access events for the requested date range. Forensic exports will follow Redwood's documented emergency export workflow and will be delivered over an agreed secure channel. Redwood warrants it will not disclose the requested export to any third party beyond the enumerated subprocessors without Customer consent, except where legally compelled.

We recommend adding a 30-day SLA to turnaround for routine access requests and a charged, expedited path for 72-hour emergency exports. I'll link the DocuSign template once Legal confirms redlines.

—Kimberly
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference

From: Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
To: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@carewell.com, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 5 Aug 2025 09:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Thanks all — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. A few follow-ups from our side before we send to procurement: 

- Can we get a sample (redacted) audit log snippet showing the subprocessor-hop metadata you mentioned? If possible, include a mock request-id and timestamps so our auditors can follow the trace.
- On retention: CareWell prefers the ability to set TTLs at the org level (default 24 hours, optional up to 90 days). Can Redwood confirm if org-level TTL configuration is feasible without an SOW? If not, procurement will flag it as an SOW item and that will slow things down.
- On SLAs: the 30-day routine/72-hour emergency timeline is reasonable; can you confirm costs for expedited forensic exports?

If you can get the sample log and a short note on cost/timeline for org-level TTL change today, procurement will try to get a draft SOW out by Friday.

Laura

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
To: Laura Chen <laura.chen@carewell.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, procurement@carewell.com
Date: Tue, 5 Aug 2025 15:44:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Operationalizing Ephemeral Sessions: Redaction & Subprocessor Chain-of-Custody

Laura — appreciate the quick turn. Quick answers and next steps: 

- Sample audit log: attached below (inline snippet). It contains a mock request-id, timestamp, model, redaction flag, and subprocessor-hop id. We'll redact any customer-identifying fields before sending production examples.

  Sample (redacted):
  { request_id: "req-3375a", timestamp: "2025-08-03T16:08:22Z", model: "rwd-llm-v2", redaction_applied: true, subprocessor_hops: ["sp-hop-01:aws-inference", "sp-hop-03:log-processor"] }

- Org-level TTL: we can expose an org-level TTL toggle in the console. Default 24 hours will remain; customers can request up to 90 days via the Console or API. Org-level toggles beyond 30 days will be subject to a pricing tier; procurement can flag the desired default and we'll include it in the SOW pricing appendix. We can implement the toggle without an SOW for pilot customers; broader rollout to all accounts will require our standard change control (1–2 week config window).

- Costs for expedited exports: standard forensic export is included as part of an enterprise support add-on (one routine export per quarter). Expedited 72-hour forensic exports are billed at the hourly incident-response rate; rough estimate for a typical export is $2,500–$6,000 depending on scope. We can provide a fixed-price doc if CareWell prefers.

Next steps: Kimberly will drop final Annex text, Marissa will include the redacted log and the subprocessor PDF (attached), and I will prepare a short SOW appendix that captures TTL options and the expedited export pricing. If that works I'll ask procurement to exchange signatures this week.

—David
Senior Privacy Manager, Redwood Inference
